title: The turn
hookLine: the turn at the end of the lane is its own practice

lines: THE TURN IS ITS OWN PRACTICE.
cards: Walking from the car to the door. Waiting for the kettle. The half-second between finishing one email and opening the next.

In-between moments, easy to treat as nothing. That's exactly where attention leaks away. On the walking lane, the in-between moment is the turn: you reach the end, and there's a little gap before you walk back.
It's easy to rush it. Swing around, done. But teachers keep saying the same surprising thing: the turn is its own practice.

teach.b: In the Burmese noting method, the turn has its own labels. You reach the end of the lane. Standing, standing: you stop and feel the whole body, kaya, upright.
Then something easy to miss: intending to turn. Before the body moves there's an intention, a tiny decision, and the practice asks you to catch it.
Then turning, turning, as the body slowly rotates, one foot at a time. Then standing again, intending to walk, and off you go. Why so much fuss about a turn?
Because it's where the mind likes to wake up and wander off. Walking in a straight line, attention can settle into a rhythm. At the turn the rhythm breaks, and the mind jumps to the next thing.

teach.h: THE BIGGER TURNS OF THE DAY.
teach.b: If you can stay present through the turn, you can stay present through the bigger turns of the day: getting up, sitting down, walking into a room, starting a new task.
Catching the intention matters in Buddhist teaching generally. Intention, cetana, is what the Buddha pointed to as the heart of action.
Noticing the small intention before a turn is practice for noticing the bigger ones before you speak or act.

And look back at this week: watching change, counting, the visitors, your own sitting, the lane, the parts of a step, and now the turn. Seven days that carried the practice from the breath to the feet.
The turn counts too, and so do all the in-between moments.

how: In the noting style of walking meditation, meditators pause at the end of the lane, note standing and the intention to turn, and turn slowly with full attention before walking back.

games.q: you reach the end of your walking lane. what do you do?
o: swing around quickly and keep going.
stop, notice the intention, and turn slowly.
games.why: standing, intending to turn, turning: the turn gets the same attention as every step.

practice: Walk slowly to the end of your few paces of floor, stop, feel yourself standing, and notice the wish to turn before you move.
Turn slowly, one small step at a time, feeling the feet shift and the body rotate; stand for a breath, notice the wish to walk, and walk back, letting each turn be as careful as each step.
If you're seated, turn your head slowly, noticing the intention first.

wordCard.voice: The turn. The moment at the end of the lane: standing, intending, turning, a practice of its own.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: intention, volition; the Buddha calls it the heart of action.

carryVoice: Your line: the turn counts too. Before the body moves, there's a choice. That's a week, from the breath to the feet.
